title: Fractions: parts, equivalence and comparison

prompts: Draw a bar to show 3/4 and another to show 6/8. Explain why they are the same amount.
Which is larger, 2/3 or 5/8? Justify your answer with a common denominator or a number line.

pedagogy.rationale: Bars, circles and the number line come before symbols; equivalence is built by splitting parts again, then used to add, subtract and compare.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Recognises equal parts of a whole.

misconceptions.description: Adds the numerators and the denominators (1/4 + 1/2 = 2/6).
misconceptions.response: The size of the parts does not change when you combine them. Make the parts the same size first.

misconceptions.description: A bigger denominator means a bigger fraction.
misconceptions.response: More parts in the same whole means each part is smaller.
5/4 is one whole and one more quarter.

misconceptions.description: Loses track of the whole (a fraction of a bag versus kilograms).
misconceptions.response: Always name the whole a fraction refers to: half of a 2 kg bag is 1 kg.

scenes.title: Sharing a kanya bar
scenes.learnerAction: Look at the shared bar and say how much has been eaten.

content.body:
Hawa cut a kanya bar into 4 equal pieces and ate 3 of them. How much of the bar did she eat? A fraction answers that question exactly.

Today you will show fractions with bars, circles and a number line, find fractions that are equal, and use them to add, subtract and compare.

accessibility.textAlternative: A kanya bar cut into 4 equal pieces, with 3 pieces shaded to show they were eaten. 3 of 4 equal pieces is the fraction three quarters.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Read the scene, then press Continue.

offline.note: The model is drawn on the device.

visual.caption: 3 of 4 equal pieces: $\frac{3}{4}$ of the bar.

scenes.title: Equal parts of a whole
scenes.learnerAction: Change the number of equal parts and shade some; read the fraction your model shows.

content.body:
A fraction names equal parts of a whole. The **denominator** (bottom) says how many equal parts the whole is cut into. The **numerator** (top) says how many of those parts you have.

A fraction can be a whole or more: $\frac{4}{4} = 1$ and $\frac{5}{4}$ is one whole and one more quarter.
keyPoints: $\frac{3}{4}$: the whole is cut into 4 equal parts and we have 3 of them.
Always name the whole: a quarter of a bar, a quarter of a 2 kg bag.

accessibility.textAlternative: A fraction names equal parts of a whole. In three quarters, the whole is cut into 4 equal parts and 3 are shaded. A circle cut into 8 equal parts with 5 shaded shows five eighths. Four quarters make one whole, and five quarters is one whole and one more quarter.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Use the More parts and Fewer parts buttons, then choose parts to shade with Tab and Space.

offline.note: The models are drawn on the device.

blocks.caption: A circle in 8 equal parts with 5 shaded: $\frac{5}{8}$.
Numerator on top, denominator below the line.

blocks.title: Fractions can be 1 or more
blocks.text: $\frac{4}{4}$ is one whole bar. $\frac{5}{4}$ is one whole bar and one more quarter of another bar.

visual.caption: Change the number of equal parts and shade some. The fraction updates to match your bar.

scenes.title: Same amount, different names
scenes.learnerAction: Split every part again and watch the fraction's name change while the amount stays the same.

content.body:
Cut every part of $\frac{1}{2}$ into 2 smaller parts: now there are 4 parts and 2 are shaded, so $\frac{1}{2} = \frac{2}{4}$. The shaded amount did not change; only the size of the parts did.

Multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number gives an **equivalent fraction**.

accessibility.textAlternative: One half of a bar is shaded. Splitting every part into 2 gives 2 of 4 parts shaded; splitting into 3 gives 3 of 6; into 4 gives 4 of 8. One half equals two quarters equals three sixths equals four eighths: the same amount with smaller parts.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Choose a split button to cut every part again.

blocks.caption: Multiply the top and bottom by the same number.

visual.caption: The shaded amount stays the same; the parts get smaller and there are more of them.

scenes.title: Worked solutions: rice and kanya
scenes.learnerAction: Reveal each step of two worked solutions: an addition and a comparison.

content.body: Watch equivalent fractions do two jobs: adding fractions with different parts, and comparing them.

accessibility.textAlternative: Example 1: Boima has a quarter of a bag of rice and buys half a bag more. Half equals two quarters, so one quarter plus two quarters is three quarters of a bag. The denominators are not added. Example 2: compare three quarters and five eighths. Three quarters equals six eighths, which is more than five eighths.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Press Show next step until every step of both examples is shown.

blocks.problem: Boima has $\frac{1}{4}$ of a bag of rice. He buys $\frac{1}{2}$ of a bag more. How much of a bag does he have now?

steps.text: The parts are different sizes: quarters and halves. Make them the same size first.
Now add the quarters. The size of the parts (quarters) does not change.
Name the whole: Boima has $\frac{3}{4}$ of a bag of rice.

blocks.problem: Which is more kanya: $\frac{3}{4}$ of a bar or $\frac{5}{8}$ of the same size of bar?

steps.text: Give both fractions the same denominator: eighths.
Compare the numerators now that the parts are the same size.
So $\frac{3}{4}$ of a bar is more than $\frac{5}{8}$ of a bar.

scenes.title: Solve with help: build and place fractions
scenes.learnerAction: Shade a bar to show a fraction, place a fraction on a number line and compare two fractions.

content.body: Use the models. If you are stuck, open the hint in the help panel.

hints: To compare, give both fractions the same denominator, or picture both bars the same length.

accessibility.textAlternative: Task 1: shade a bar of 6 equal parts to show two thirds; four of six parts is two thirds. Task 2: place three quarters on a number line from 0 to 1 marked in quarters. Task 3: compare two thirds and three quarters; two thirds is eight twelfths and three quarters is nine twelfths, so two thirds is less.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each part and press Space to shade it; use the arrow keys to move the point on the number line; choose less than, equal to or greater than.

blocks.caption: Shade the bar to show $\frac{2}{3}$. You may change the number of parts.

scenes.title: Solve with help: add and subtract
scenes.learnerAction: Add and subtract fractions with related denominators, using the hints if needed.

content.body: Make the parts the same size, then add or subtract the numerators. Type answers as fractions, such as 3/4.

hints: Which denominator can both fractions be written in? Eighths work for halves, quarters and eighths.

accessibility.textAlternative: Problem 1: one quarter plus one half. Write one half as two quarters; the answer is three quarters. Problem 2: five eighths minus one quarter. Write one quarter as two eighths; the answer is three eighths.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each answer box, type a fraction and press Check.

blocks.prompt: Work out each one. Write the answer as a fraction.

misconceptions.feedback: You added the tops and the bottoms (2/6). The parts must be the same size first: $\frac{1}{2} = \frac{2}{4}$, so $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{2}{4}$.
You subtracted the tops and the bottoms (4/4). Write the quarter as eighths first: $\frac{1}{4} = \frac{2}{8}$.

scenes.title: Try it alone
scenes.learnerAction: Add, subtract, compare and place fractions without hints.

content.body: No hints this time. Each solution appears after you check.

accessibility.textAlternative: Work out three eighths plus one half, and five sixths minus one third. Compare seven twelfths with two thirds. Place five quarters on a number line from 0 to 2.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each task; type fractions, choose a comparison, and move the point with the arrow keys.

blocks.prompt: Write each answer as a fraction.

misconceptions.feedback: 4/10 adds the tops and the bottoms. Write the half as eighths first.
4/3 subtracts the tops and the bottoms. Write the third as sixths first.

scenes.title: Find the mistakes
scenes.learnerAction: Diagnose a wrong addition and answer three questions that catch common fraction mistakes.

content.body: These answers come from real ways of thinking that do not quite work. Find what went wrong.

accessibility.textAlternative: Jallah wrote one quarter plus one half equals two sixths, adding the tops and the bottoms. The parts must be made the same size first; the answer is three quarters. Further questions: which is bigger, one eighth or one quarter (one quarter); how much is five quarters of a bar (one whole bar and a quarter); and what is half of a 2 kilogram bag of rice (1 kilogram).
accessibility.keyboardPath: Choose one option for each question with the arrow keys and Space.

blocks.question: What went wrong?

options.text: Jallah added the denominators. The parts must be the same size before adding.
options.feedback: Yes. $\frac{2}{6}$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$ on its own, which cannot be right. $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{2}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$.
Multiplying is a different operation. The question asks for the total of the two amounts.
Check the size: $\frac{2}{6}$ is smaller than $\frac{1}{2}$, but we added more to the half.

correction: Make the parts the same size: $\frac{1}{2} = \frac{2}{4}$.

items.prompt: Which is bigger: $\frac{1}{8}$ of a bar or $\frac{1}{4}$ of the same bar?

options.feedback: Yes. Cutting the bar into 8 parts makes each part smaller than cutting it into 4.
A bigger denominator means more parts, so each part is smaller. $\frac{1}{8}$ is half of $\frac{1}{4}$.
Both have one part, but the parts are different sizes.

items.prompt: Musu ate $\frac{5}{4}$ kanya bars. How much is that?

options.text: One whole bar and one quarter of another
options.feedback: Yes. $\frac{4}{4}$ is one whole bar, and one more quarter makes $\frac{5}{4}$.

options.text: That is impossible: a fraction is less than 1
options.feedback: Fractions can be 1 or more. $\frac{5}{4}$ is more than one whole.
5 quarters is more than 4 quarters, and 4 quarters is a whole bar.

items.prompt: A bag of rice weighs 2 kg. How much rice is in half of the bag?

options.feedback: Yes. The whole is 2 kg, and half of 2 kg is 1 kg.
Half of the bag is not half of a kilogram. The whole here is the 2 kg bag.
$\frac{2}{2}$ is one whole. Name the whole first: half of a 2 kg bag.

scenes.title: Apply it: palm oil at the market
scenes.learnerAction: Solve a new market problem that needs adding, comparing and naming the whole.

content.body: Ma Fatu sells palm oil in litres. Use what you learned to answer her questions.

accessibility.textAlternative: Ma Fatu has three quarters of a litre of palm oil in one bottle and one half of a litre in another. How much oil does she have altogether? Can it all fit in a 1 litre bottle?
accessibility.keyboardPath: Type the total, press Check, then choose an answer.

blocks.prompt: Ma Fatu has $\frac{3}{4}$ L of palm oil in one bottle and $\frac{1}{2}$ L in another. How many litres does she have altogether? Write a fraction or a mixed number.

misconceptions.feedback: 4/6 adds the tops and the bottoms. Write the half as quarters first.

items.prompt: Can all of Ma Fatu's oil fit into one 1 L bottle?

options.text: No: $\frac{5}{4}$ L is more than 1 L
options.feedback: Yes. $\frac{5}{4}$ L is $1\frac{1}{4}$ L, a quarter of a litre more than the bottle holds.

options.text: Yes: fractions are always less than 1
options.feedback: A total of fractions can be more than 1. $\frac{4}{4}$ L fills the bottle and $\frac{1}{4}$ L is left over.
$\frac{4}{4}$ L would fill it exactly. She has $\frac{5}{4}$ L.

scenes.title: Remember
scenes.learnerAction: Recall how equivalent fractions help you add and compare.

content.body: Say each point aloud before the check.
keyPoints: A fraction names equal parts of a named whole; it can be 1 or more.
Multiply the top and bottom by the same number for an equivalent fraction.
Make the parts the same size before you add, subtract or compare.

accessibility.textAlternative: A fraction names equal parts of a named whole and can be 1 or more. Multiplying the top and bottom by the same number gives an equivalent fraction. Make the parts the same size before adding, subtracting or comparing. A question asks which fraction equals three quarters: six eighths.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Choose one option with the arrow keys and Space.

options.feedback: Yes: multiply the top and bottom by 2.
Adding 1 to the top and bottom does not keep the amount the same.
Eighths are smaller than quarters, so 3 eighths is less than 3 quarters.

scenes.title: Show what you know
scenes.learnerAction: Answer the assessment questions on your own.

content.body: Now show what you can do on your own. The assessment is checked by your teacher's assessment system, not by this lesson.

accessibility.textAlternative: The assessment asks you to represent, add, subtract and compare fractions on your own. It is delivered by the assessment player.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Answer each assessment question, then submit.
